study.title: Jonah 4 - The mercy of God and the anger of the prophet
study.overview: The final chapter of Jonah shows the contrast between the heart of God and the heart of the prophet. Jonah is deeply contradicted because Nineveh is not destroyed; but God exposes the spiritual narrowness of the prophet through a plant, an insect and the scorching wind. The chapter ends with an open divine question: if Jonah feels compassion for something passing and who has not cultivated, the more God would have compassion on the great city with his inhabitants and animals. The text emphasizes God's sovereign freedom in showing mercy and the need for God's servant to align his affections with the character of the Lord.

outline.title: The irritation of Jonah in the face of divine mercy
outline.explanation: Jonah does not rejoice at the deliverance of Nineveh; rather, his reaction is of strong disgust and anger. He reveals that he had fled because he knew that God is gracious, merciful, patient, and willing to forgive evil when there is repentance. The central problem is not ignorance, but moral resistance to the merciful character of God.

outline.title: The desire to die and the question of the Lord
outline.explanation: Jonah prefers death to submission to the will of God. The Lord answers with a question that confronts the legitimacy of this anger. Dialogue shows that God not only acts with mercy, but also disciplines the prophet with questions that expose his heart.

outline.title: The lesson of the plant, caterpillar and hot wind
outline.explanation: Jonah retreats to observe the city, as God successively prepares a plan for shade, a caterpillar to destroy it and a scorching eastern wind to afflict it. The prophet rejoices in passenger comfort and returns to desire death when he is taken away. The narrative uses Jonas' personal experience to reveal his selective compassion.

outline.title: The conclusion: compassion for Nineveh
outline.explanation: God shows Jonah's incoherence: he feels pity on a plant that he has not grown, but does not want God to pity an entire city. The argument culminates in Nineveh, a great city with many morally ignorant people and many animals. The end remains in the form of a question, inviting the reader to agree with the compassion of God.

study.context: The chapter presupposes Jonah's previous mission to Nineveh and the city's reply of repentance in chapter 3. The notes provided highlight that Jonah knew from the beginning the graceful character of the LORD, associated with the formula of Exodus 34:6-7. The contrast between Israel and the nations is also important: God was already acting to bring salvation beyond Israel, and Nineveh appears as an example of a city attained by the prophetic word. The text does not offer additional historical details beyond these literary and theological elements.
study.theology: Jonah 4 teaches that God's mercy is not a deviation from his holiness, but an expression of his own character. The prophet quotes, in essence, the revealed character of the LORD: gracious, compassionate, late in anger and ready to reverse judgment when there is repentance. At the same time, the chapter denounces a religious heart that accepts mercy for itself, but resists when it reaches enemies. The final question shows that God values people, including those who do not distinguish good and evil clearly, and also considers animals under their providence. Theologically, the book ends by stating that God prefers to save destroy, and that his servants should learn to rejoice in the grace given to others, including those who were seen as enemies.

scholarViews.insight: Jonah knew from the beginning that the LORD would not destroy the Ninevites if they repented; their escape was motivated by the conscience of the merciful character of God.
Jonah's wrath is condemned because he clings to his own prestige and unfulfilled prediction, rather than to rejoice in the goodness and mercy of God.

questions: Why can Jonah value both his personal comfort and so little God's mercy to Nineveh?
In what situations do I get bored when God does good to people I would prefer to see judged?
How can I learn to celebrate God's grace when it reaches people I consider difficult or unlikely?
study.practice: Examine whether there is in you the same selectivity of Jonah: compassion for what benefits you and hardness in the face of the restoration of others. Pray for the Lord to align your feelings with his, especially when the grace of God reaches people you did not expect. Practise to thank not only for the mercy received, but also for the mercy granted to others, remembering that God's goal is to save, and not destroy, when there is repentance.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not accurately identify which Jonah group had in mind when he mentions that the inhabitants of Nineveh did not distinguish the right from the left; the most natural reading is of moral or spiritual ignorance, but the text and notes no longer detail. There are also no elements in the notes to safely define whether the reference to animals has only arguing function or also expanded literal compassion, although both ideas are compatible with the verse.
